Margaret Floy Washburn

American psychologist, the first woman to earn a doctorate in psychology (Cornell, 1894). Her book The Animal Mind was a standard text in comparative psychology.

Biography

Margaret Floy Washburn was born in New York in 1871. She wanted to study with James McKeen Cattell at Columbia, which did not admit women to graduate study; she attended as a guest and, on Cattell's own advice, moved to Cornell. There, under Edward Titchener, she earned her doctorate in 1894, the first woman to receive a PhD in psychology. She taught for more than three decades at Vassar College, where she supervised many research projects by her students. She died in 1939.

Questions she investigated

  • What can we infer about other animals' experience from their behaviour?
  • What role do movements, even tiny ones, play in thinking and imagination?

Contributions

The Animal Mind (1908) gathered and critically organised what was known about perception, learning and behaviour in very different species, from single-celled organisms to mammals. It went through several editions and served as a textbook for a quarter of a century. In Movement and Mental Imagery (1916) she proposed that consciousness is tied to motor tendencies, an idea seeking common ground between introspection and behaviourism.

She was president of the American Psychological Association in 1921 and in 1931 became the second woman elected to the US National Academy of Sciences.

Criticism, limits and reception

Her approach, which allowed careful inferences about the animal mind, ran against the current when behaviourism proposed sticking to behaviour alone. Comparative psychology and the study of animal cognition have since returned to many of her questions.

References

  1. Washburn, M. F. (1908). The Animal Mind: A Text-Book of Comparative Psychology. Nueva York: Macmillan.
  2. Scarborough, E. y Furumoto, L. (1987). Untold Lives: The First Generation of American Women Psychologists. Columbia University Press.
